SEC22A-01.explanation: The subject is "wild oat seeds," whose head noun "seeds" is plural; the phrase "as well as the occasional seed of field bindweed" is set off by commas and does not join the subject, so the singular "seed" and "bindweed" beside the blank do not control the verb. The verb must therefore be plural. The next sentence, "Nobody sows or waters them; the seeds simply sprout on their own," shows that no one acts on the seeds, so the verb must be active and used without an object: "germinate." "germinates" is active but singular, agreeing with "seed" in the interrupting phrase. "are germinated" is plural but passive, implying an agent that the final sentence rules out. "is germinated" is both singular and passive.

SEC22A-02.explanation: The subject is "A number of the delta's rice growers." "A number of" means "several" and takes a plural verb, so the head word "number" does not make the subject singular; the verb must be plural, agreeing with "growers." The next sentence states the result in the present tense: "Their paddies emit markedly less methane" and "their harvests are no smaller." A past change whose consequence holds in the present calls for the present perfect, so the answer is "have adapted." "has adapted" has the right aspect but is singular, treating "number" as the subject. "were adapting" is plural but past progressive, describing an action in progress at some past moment that the passage never establishes, which does not fit the present-tense result. "was adapting" is both singular and past progressive.

SEC22A-03.explanation: The subject is "hydroponics," the name of a growing method; although it ends in -s, it is a singular noun, like "genetics," so the verb must be singular. The sentences that follow describe a current practice in the present tense: the method "can cut" water use, the rest "flows" back, and "Growers on those farms add mineral salts" and "adjust the mixture." The verb must therefore be present: "is practiced." "are practiced" is present but plural, treating the -s ending as a plural marker. "was practiced" is singular but past, which would place the farming in the past even though the last sentence says the growers on those same farms add salts today. "were practiced" is both plural and past.

SEC22A-04.explanation: The subject is "a spheroid"; the phrase "its outer cells wrapped in a thin sheath of collagen" is an absolute phrase with its own noun, "cells," and is not part of the subject, so the verb must be singular. The next sentence says that "its growth halts" within hours of the dose, so the growth was already under way when the researchers "add" the drug and is interrupted by it; an action in progress at the moment another event occurs takes the progressive: "is proliferating." "proliferates" is singular but simple present; with "when the researchers add" it would mean the spheroid starts growing in response to the drug, which contradicts the halt. "are proliferating" is progressive but plural, agreeing with "cells" in the absolute phrase. "proliferate" is both plural and simple.

SEC22A-05.explanation: The blank is the verb of the relative clause "that the bird ______," whose subject is "the bird," not "The fig seeds"; the seeds are the antecedent of "that." Because "bird" is singular, the verb must be singular. In that clause "that" stands for the seeds and is the verb's object, and the last sentence confirms that the bird is the one carrying the seeds, since it "swallowed figs" in one place and "dropped their seeds" in another. The verb must therefore be active: "was depositing." "were depositing" is active but plural, agreeing with "seeds." "was deposited" is singular but passive; it would make the bird the thing deposited and leave "that" with no role in the clause. "were deposited" is both plural and passive.

SEC22A-06.explanation: The subject is "The plasma units," whose head noun "units" is plural; "collected from one donor with an unusual antibody" is a reduced relative clause that modifies "units," so the singular "donor" and "antibody" beside the blank do not control the verb. The verb must be plural. The first sentence names who does the testing: "Technicians at a regional blood bank test donated plasma," so the units are tested rather than doing any testing, and the verb must be passive: "have been screened." "have screened" is plural but active; it would say the units screened something, and "four separate times" is not an object. "has been screened" is passive but singular, agreeing with "antibody." "has screened" is both singular and active.

SEC22A-07.explanation: In the second half of the comparison, "the more foraging bees" is the fronted object and "a single plant" is the subject, so the verb must agree with the singular "plant," not with "bees." The two halves of a "the more ..., the more ..." comparison are parallel, and the first half uses the simple present: "the flower heads secrete"; the next sentence also uses the simple present: "The most heavily visited plants go on to produce." The verb must therefore be simple present and singular: "attracts." "attract" is simple present but plural, agreeing with the fronted "bees" or copying the plural "secrete." "has attracted" is singular but present perfect, which breaks the parallel with "secrete." "have attracted" is both plural and perfect.

SEC22A-08.explanation: The relative pronoun "which" refers to "samplers," the head of "The county's automated wastewater samplers"; "county's" is only a possessor, so the verb must be plural. The second sentence says that "the samplers continue to draw water around the clock," and the main clause says they "give" officials warnings in the present, so the operation began in the past and is still going on; that calls for the present perfect progressive: "have been operating." "has been operating" has the right form but is singular, agreeing with "county's." "were operating" is plural but past progressive, which places the operation in a past period and does not fit samplers that "continue" to run. "was operating" is both singular and past.

SEC22B-01.explanation: The subject is "piezometers"; "the night technician could reach without a boat" is a relative clause with its own singular subject, so neither "technician" nor "boat" controls the main verb, which must be plural. The passage narrates a finished episode in the past: the reservoir "filled," the engineers "opened" relief wells, and the pressure "leveled off," so the verb must be past: "were recording." "was recording" is past but singular, agreeing with "technician" or "boat" inside the relative clause. "are recording" is plural but present, which clashes with the past-tense account of what happened during the filling. "is recording" is both singular and present.

SEC22B-02.explanation: The subject is "wires"; "because the protective zinc coating has worn away" is an adverbial clause with its own singular subject and verb, so "coating" and "has" do not control the main verb, which must be plural. The wires do not attack anything: nothing after the blank is an object, and the sentence names the attacker in "by hydrogen that forms as the bare metal corrodes," eight words after the blank, so the verb must be passive: "are being attacked." "is being attacked" is passive but singular, agreeing with "coating" (or "bridge") rather than "wires." "are attacking" is plural but active, which would make the wires the attackers and leaves the verb with no object while "by hydrogen" names the real agent. "is attacking" is both singular and active.

SEC22B-03.explanation: The subject is "slab"; "of granite on the eastern face of the ridge above the valley's hiking trails" is a chain of prepositional phrases, so the plural "trails" just before the blank does not control the verb, which must be singular. The next sentence says the slab "remains attached at its base" while the fracture "widens," so the separation is still in progress, not complete: "is detaching." "has detached" is singular but present perfect, saying the slab has already come away, which contradicts "remains attached." "are detaching" is progressive but plural, agreeing with "trails." "have detached" is plural and also says the separation is complete.

SEC22B-04.explanation: The subject is "alignment"; "the northern heading and the southern heading" is a compound inside the prepositional phrase "between ...," not a compound subject, so the verb must be singular. The checking happened only while the machines "advanced toward each other," and the next sentence closes that period: the machines "broke through" and the halves "met," so the verb must be simple past: "was checked." "has been checked" is singular but present perfect, which wrongly ties a finished, closed-off period of surveying to the present. "were checked" is past but plural, treating the two headings as the subject. "have been checked" is both plural and present perfect.

SEC22B-05.explanation: After "nor," the auxiliary comes before the subject, and the subject here is "instrument," five words later, not the plural "stations" of the first clause, so the auxiliary must be singular. The main verb of this clause is the base form "measure," ten words after the blank, and a base form needs the auxiliary "do," not "have" (which would need "measured"): "does the." "do the" uses the right auxiliary but is plural, copying the number of "stations." "has the" is singular but takes the perfect auxiliary, which cannot combine with "measure." "have the" copies the first clause's "have never sampled" in both number and auxiliary.

SEC22B-06.explanation: "The latter" refers to the second of the two kinds of track named in the first sentence, "long wrought-iron rails," which is plural, so the verb must be plural even though "latter" looks like a single item. The passage describes a finished historical period: engineers "tried" both kinds, the cast rails "cracked," and every line "had replaced" them, so the verb must be simple past: "were costlier." "was costlier" is past but singular, treating "the latter" as one thing. "have been costlier" is plural but present perfect, which wrongly connects a closed episode in early railway history to the present. "has been costlier" is both singular and present perfect.

SEC22B-07.explanation: The subject is "moon"; "spacecraft measurements suggest" is a comment clause set off by commas, so its plural subject "measurements" does not control the main verb, which must be singular. After the interrupter "through a set of long fractures near the pole," the verb takes a direct object, "towering jets of water vapor and salty ice grains," so the moon is doing the ejecting and the verb must be active: "has been ejecting." "has been ejected" is singular but passive, which would make the moon itself the thing ejected and leave "towering jets" with no grammatical role. "have been ejecting" is active but plural, agreeing with "measurements." "have been ejected" is both plural and passive.

SEC22B-08.explanation: The subject is "Attempts"; "by a single amateur astronomer to measure the brightness of its scattered fragments" modifies it, so "astronomer" and "brightness" do not control the verb, which must be plural. The documenting is finished, not in progress: the paper that holds the tables is one that a journal "accepted and printed," and it "became" the standard record, so the verb must be simple present passive describing what the finished paper contains: "are documented." "are being documented" is plural but progressive, as if the tables were still being compiled, which contradicts "printed." "is documented" is simple but singular, agreeing with "astronomer" or "brightness." "is being documented" is both singular and progressive.

SEC22C-01.explanation: The subject is "questionnaire," a singular noun; "the statisticians'" is only a possessive describing whose questionnaire it is, so it cannot be the subject, and the verb must be singular. The verb must also be present perfect: the state began at a past point, "from the season it was printed," and still holds, as the present-tense "borrow" in the same sentence shows, so only "has been indispensable" spans that interval. "have been indispensable" has the right aspect but is plural, agreeing with the possessive "statisticians'." "is indispensable" is singular, but the simple present cannot reach back to a starting point in the past ("from the season it was printed"). "are indispensable" is both plural and in the wrong tense.

SEC22C-02.explanation: The blank is the second verb of a compound predicate whose subject is "teachers," at the start of the sentence, so the verb must be plural; "schoolmistress," the singular noun just before "and," belongs to the first predicate ("transcribed the water-stained diary of its last schoolmistress") and is not a subject. The action must also be a completed one, not an ongoing one: it is paired with the simple, completed "transcribed," and the next sentence says the registries "stopped accepting entries two winters ago," so no contributing can still be in progress. Only "have contributed" is plural and completed. "have been contributing" is plural but describes an activity continuing up to now, which a registry that stopped accepting entries two winters ago rules out. "has contributed" is completed but singular, as if "schoolmistress" were the subject. "has been contributing" is both singular and progressive.

SEC22C-03.explanation: Inside the relative clause, the subject of the blank is "scripts" ("whose unsigned scripts"), which is plural; "playwright" is the subject of the main clause, whose verb is "wrote," not of the relative clause, so the verb must be plural. The verb must also be past: the frame is a past narrative, with "kept" in the first sentence, "wrote" and "never attended" in the playwright's own clause, and "memorized" and "burned" in the last sentence. Only "were being passed" is plural and past. "are being passed" is plural but present, which clashes with "wrote" and the rest of the past narrative. "was being passed" is past but singular, agreeing with "playwright." "is being passed" is both singular and present.

SEC22C-04.explanation: "which" here refers to the whole action of the preceding clause, the conservator's stripping of the varnish; that action is what can be recorded "as a separate treatment," whereas "owners," the plural noun just before the comma, cannot be a treatment. A clause used as an antecedent takes a singular verb. The verb must also be simple present: the sentence describes a routine that recurs "Whenever a museum lends" a painting, and the next sentence continues that routine in the present tense ("read," "compare," "goes"), so the logging is part of each repetition rather than a single completed event. Only "is logged" is singular and simple present. "has been logged" is singular but presents the logging as one finished event, which does not fit a procedure repeated whenever a painting is lent. "are logged" is simple present but plural, as if "owners" were the antecedent. "have been logged" is both plural and perfect.

SEC22C-05.explanation: The relative clause "that ______ as part of the river god's escort" describes "boys," not "priest": the next sentence says the priest "wears his everyday black cassock," so he is not in costume, and the verb must agree with the plural "boys." The verb must also be passive: the boys do not dress themselves, because their grandmothers "sew the costumes" and "fit them onto the boys before dawn," so by the time the boys carry torches in the procession they have been dressed by someone else. Only "are dressed" is plural and passive. "are dressing" is plural but active and progressive, saying the boys are putting on costumes themselves during the procession, which the grandmothers' fitting before dawn rules out. "is dressed" is passive but singular, attaching the clause to "priest," whom the cassock sentence excludes. "is dressing" is both singular and active.

SEC22C-06.explanation: The subject is "script," which is singular; "unlike those of the puppeteers' lavish marionette dramas" is a comparison phrase set off by commas, and neither "those" nor "dramas" is the subject, so the verb must be singular. The verb must also be present perfect progressive: the activity covers a span that began in the past, "each of the seasons that followed its premiere," and it continues, as the present-tense "write" shows. Only "has been traveling" is singular and spans that interval. "is traveling" is singular, but the present progressive describes only the present moment and cannot cover seasons that "followed" the premiere in the past. "have been traveling" has the right aspect but is plural, agreeing with "those" or "dramas." "are traveling" is both plural and in the wrong aspect.

SEC22C-07.explanation: The subject is "claim," which is singular; "that the abbey's monks had forged their own land charters" is a clause explaining the claim, and its own subject "monks" and the plural "charters" just before the blank belong to that clause, so the verb must be singular. The verb must also be active: the next sentence says the rivals "never needed to promote it" and that the accusation "spread by itself," so the claim is the thing moving through the marketplaces, not something that anyone was distributing. Only "was circulating" is singular and active. "was being circulated" is singular but passive, implying someone was deliberately passing the claim around, which the second sentence denies. "were circulating" is active but plural, agreeing with "monks" or "charters." "were being circulated" is both plural and passive.

SEC22C-08.explanation: The sentence is inverted: the fronted phrase "Complicating any attempt to credit the panel to one master or to his assistants" is not the subject, and the subject follows the verb, "the faint and partly scraped initials," whose head noun "initials" is plural; "attempt," "panel," and "master" are singular but sit inside the fronted phrase, so the verb must be plural. The verb must also be present: the dispute is a current one, with "disagree" in the first sentence and "read" and "dismiss" in the last, so the initials complicate attribution now. Only "are the" is plural and present. "were the" is plural but past, which clashes with the present-tense dispute around it. "is the" is present but singular, as if "attempt" or the fronted phrase were the subject. "was the" is both singular and past.
